ce:caption.ce:simple-para: Concept of eradicating CML LSCs by TM5614 combined with TKI
A. CML is characterized by a marked proliferation of differentiated myeloid cells, whereas CML LSCs are in a quiescent stage in the bone marrow niche.

B. TKIs inhibit proliferation of CML cells, leading to apoptosis. CML LSCs remain because they are not sensitive to TKIs. Discontinuation of TKI causes CML cell differentiation and proliferation again from CML LSCs

C. If TKI is combined with TM5614, CML LSCs in the quiescent phase enter cell cycle, become TKI sensitive, and are eradicated by TKI. CML does not relapse after discontinuation of TKI and restoration of normal hematopoiesis by normal clones is observed.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: The new treatment goal for chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is treatment-free remission, which requires the achievement and maintenance of a deep molecular response (DMR) using a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI). However, only a limited number of patients achieve or maintain DMR. TM5614, a PAI1 inhibitor, can bring quiescent hematopoietic stem cells from the bone marrow niche into the cell cycle. Thus, the combination of TM5614 and TKI may eradicate CML cells. Currently, a phase III clinical trial is confirming the efficacy of TM5614 and TKI combination therapy.

ce:section.ce:para: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a hematopoietic neoplasm in which myeloid cells differentiate from CML stem cells (CML LSCs) carrying the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene, resulting from the reciprocal translocation of chromosomes 9 and 22 of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and proliferate autonomously through BCR::ABL1 tyrosine kinase activity. The primary aim of CML treatment should be to ensure a normal life expectancy for patients with CML, and this can be achieved by preventing disease progression to blast crisis (BC); in untreated cases, BC occurs in approximately 5 years, and the long-term prognosis is poor despite HSC transplantation [1].

Since the clinical application of imatinib in 2001, the prognosis of CML has significantly improved [2,3]. Tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) inhibit CML cell proliferation by competitively binding to the ATP-binding site and inhibiting BCR::ABL1 tyrosine kinase phosphorylation. If the BCR::ABL1-positive clone has decreased to at least a major molecular response (MMR) (BCR::ABL1 international Scale [IS] ≤ 0.1 %), it is unlikely to progress to BC if TKI administration is continued [4]. Second- and third-generation TKIs with strong inhibitory activity of BCR::ABL1 tyrosine kinase and efficacy against imatinib-resistant ABL point mutations have been developed, and TKIs have become the standard of therapy for CML [5–7]. In addition to TKIs, asciminib, the first member of a new class of drugs, namely STAMP inhibitors, is now available for the treatment of CML patients who have received at least two previous TKIs [8]. Currently, the life expectancy of patients with CML has improved and has no difference compared with the general population adjusted for age [9]

CML LSCs, which are believed to be latent and quiescent in the bone marrow (BM) niche, are insensitive to TKIs [10,11]. Therefore, it was believed that TKI administration was necessary for life and could not be discontinued, leading to TKI-related adverse effects, decreased physical and mental quality of life (QoL), and medical economic burden. Furthermore, some mathematical models suggest that >30 years of continuous treatment is required to completely deplete CML cells and treatment interruption would be realistically impossible [12,13] (see Fig. 1A and 1B).

However, in 2010, Mahon et al. reported in France that some patients with CML receiving long-term TKI therapy were free of molecular genetic relapse after TKI discontinuation, which is currently defined as treatment-free remission (TFR) [14]. Subsequently, several prospective trials, including the JALSG STIM213 trial, showed that a TFR could be achieved in patients treated with long-term TKI therapy [15–19]. This study investigated which patients with CML could discontinue TKIs and found that, besides a sufficient duration of TKI treatment, a certain duration of deep molecular response (DMR), a state of molecular remission deeper than MMR, was required. DMR was defined by MR4 [BCR::ABL1 IS ≤ 0.01 %] or MR4.5 [BCR::ABL1 IS ≤ 0.0032 %] depending on the sensitivity of IS-PCR.

If TKI was discontinued for intolerance or other reasons despite the level of MMR, molecular relapse was observed. Particularly, DMR is the first milestone in obtaining TFR, and TFR is impossible without DMR. Currently, the NCCN Guidelines [20], ELN 2020 recommendations [21], and JSH practical guidelines for hematological malignancies [22] have established TFR as a new treatment goal for CML, with the requirement of achieving DMR and its maintenance for ≥2 years to reach TFR.

In a phase III trial of nilotinib, a second-generation TKI for newly diagnosed patients with chronic-phase CML, the five-year cumulative DMR in the nilotinib group was 52 % (31 % for imatinib) and reached a plateau after five years, whereas the 10-year cumulative DMR was only 61.2 % (39.2 % for imatinib). The two-year DMR continuation rate was 48.9 % for nilotinib (31.4 % for control imatinib) [23]. Dasatinib, another second-generation TKI, has a five-year cumulative DMR achievement rate of 42 % (33 % for control imatinib) [24]. According to the BFORE study on second-generation bosutinib, the five-year cumulative DMR achievement rate was 46 % (35.4 % for imatinib controls) [25]. Although there were no long-term observations, the two-year DMR continuation rates for dasatinib and bosutinib were estimated to be almost the same as those for nilotinib. Accordingly, the cumulative DMR rate by the fifth year of TKI treatment is 5–12 % annually, and 80–85 % of these patients will remain on DMR for two years. Particularly, it was estimated that despite long-term TKI treatment, only ≤50 % of newly diagnosed patients with CML would be candidates for TFR.

TM5614 is a lead compound for PAI-1 inhibitors obtained by structure-based drug design technology based on the X-ray crystallographic information of human PAI-1. PAI-1 inhibitors only lyse intravascular thrombi via endogenous tPA, activating the fibrinolytic system; therefore, they are believed to have a different mechanism of action than conventional agents that inhibit thrombogenesis. The fibrinolytic system is important in vascular remodeling and cell migration and has been reported to be involved in HSCs differentiation, proliferation, and migration in the BM environment. We observed that multiple doses of PAI-1 inhibitors during transplantation of BM or human HSCs into wild-type or immunocompromised mice caused HSCs to leave the BM niche, promote their differentiation into blood cells, and markedly enhance the regenerative response of hematopoiesis.

The discovery that TM5614 wean hematopoietic stem cells from the BM niche and promote cell differentiation led to the idea of the “CML cure” method, in which CML LSCs are weaned from the niche and differentiated CML cells are eradicated with TKIs. We demonstrated that combined TKI imatinib and TM5614 in a mouse model of CML significantly enhanced the eradication of CML cells in the BM and prolonged the survival of CML mice. Combined therapy with imatinib and TM5614 prevented the recurrence of CML-like disease in serially transplanted recipients, indicating elimination of CML LSCs [26]. Notably, PAI-1 expression is markedly upregulated in human CML stem cells (unpublished data by Dr. Takashi Yahata). This suggests that small doses of TM5614 combined with TKI can lead only CML stem cells to the active phase, allowing TKI to eradicate CML. Additionally, the drug effects of PAI-1 inhibitors are different from those of other approaches to CML stem cells, in that they do not directly kill CML stem cells and are considered safe for normal and normal stem cells (see Fig. 1C).

ce:section.ce:section-title: TM5614 phase I study and TM5614 phase II study part 1
ce:section.ce:para: In a phase I clinical study in healthy male adult, the safety and linearity of the area under the curve (AUC) of blood concentration in single oral doses ranging from 30 to 240 mg were confirmed. All adverse events that occurred at repeated doses of 60 and 120 mg were mild. Based on the pharmacokinetics simulation, it was estimated that the trough value of the blood concentration of TM5614 would reach a steady state after seven days of administration.

Thus, we conducted a phase II clinical trial (investigator-initiated clinical trial) to confirm the safety and efficacy of TM5614 combined with the first- or second-generation TKI to develop a new treatment to achieve TFR in chronic CML. The four-week combination therapy with TM5614 and TKI was found to be safe and achieved DMR in some cases. However, DMR disappeared shortly after the study. These results suggest that although combined TM5614 and TKI is safe and effective, long-term use of the combination is necessary to maintain efficacy, considering the cellular turnover of CML LSCs. Therefore, a phase II study part 2 was conducted to confirm the safety and efficacy of TM5614 in a 48-week long-term combination therapy.

This study enrolled 33 patients with chronic-phase CML treated with a stable daily dose of the first- or second-generation TKIs for at least one year and yielding MMR but not achieving MR4.5. After inclusion, patients received TM5614 and TKI. The cumulative MR4.5 incidence by 12 months as the primary endpoint was 33.3 % (95 % confidence interval; 18.0–51.8 %). The cumulative MR4.5, spontaneous conversion over 12 months was approximately 8 % with TKIs alone based on historical controls. The primary endpoint met the target of 33 % set for this trial. The half-life of BCR::ABL1 IS value at two months was significantly shorter in patients who achieved an MR4.5, of 12 months than in other patients (cutoff value; 48 days, sensitivity; 0.80, specificity; 0.91, AUC of receiver operating characteristic curve; 0.83). Here, bleeding events and abnormal coagulation related to the drug were not reported and TM5614 was found to be safe. Based on these results, we determined the efficacy and safety of TM5614 combined with TKI for 48 weeks. Furthermore, the analysis of patients who achieved DMR in this study revealed that the DMR achievement rate was significantly higher (50 %) in patients who had been treated with TKIs for 3–5 years [27].

CML is a rare disease with an estimated 1300 new cases annually (1 per 100,000 people) and approximately 15,000 patients in Japan, according to the Japanese Society of Hematology's Disease Registry Project. Therefore, it is difficult to conduct a pivotal study on a large number of patients. Therefore, we planned a phase III investigator-initiated clinical trial, a multicenter, double-blind, group-comparative study, as a pivotal study for new drug applications.

The primary endpoint was to verify that the “two-year DMR continuation rate” was significantly higher in TKI + TM5614 group compared to TKI + placebo group, and the secondary endpoint was to evaluate the “one-year cumulative DMR rate.” The eligibility criteria were patients with chronic phase CML who had been treated with a TKI for ≥3 years, had not changed TKIs or doses in the 12 weeks before enrollment, and had achieved MMR but not MR 4.5. The two-year DMR continuation rate was set at 10.2 % for the control group based on data from TKI monotherapy development trials and 42.5 % for the TM5614 combination group based on phase II studies. With an alpha error of 0.05 (bilateral) and beta error of 0.2, the statistically required number of cases was 28 per group, and the target number of cases was set at 30 per group, for 60 cases in both groups. The clinical trial is scheduled to run between April 2022 and September 2026. The required number of patients was enrolled and randomized into two groups, and the protocol treatment was continued. The clinical trial is progressing well, although its efficacy cannot be estimated because of the double-blind nature of the study.

These clinical trials were conducted to develop a treatment that will achieve the TFR milestone of DMR in all patients with CML. Successful TFR is one of the goals of CML treatment following DMR, so TFR should be challenged and observed long-term after achieving DMR. The unique mechanism of action of TM5614 may deplete CML cells and bring patients with CML who cannot be cured by TKI alone closer to a true cure.
